modern_osis:
Original heading

The psalmist's humility. Believers encouraged to trust in God.

A quiet heart before the Lord

The psalmist did not aim at worldly greatness.

He wanted to be content in whatever circumstances God assigned him.

Humble believers think less highly of themselves than other people think of them.

When love for God rules the heart, it weakens selfish pride.

A proud heart often shows itself through a proud expression.

Knowing God and understanding our duties is already learning enough to occupy our lives well.

Wisdom keeps us from meddling with things that do not belong to us.

The psalmist was willing to accept any condition in which the Lord placed him.

He had become like a young child being weaned, content to remain entirely under God's direction just as a child depends upon a mother or nurse.

We must become like little children (Matthew 18:3).

Our hearts naturally cry out for worldly possessions and pleasures.

But as grace makes the soul holy, it gradually weans us from those desires.

A child being weaned may complain and grow restless.

Soon, however, the longing for milk fades, and the child can receive more substantial food.

In a similar way, a renewed soul learns to be quiet when deprived of favorite comforts or disappointed in cherished hopes.

When circumstances do not match our wishes, we should learn to bring our wishes into submission to our circumstances.

Then we find rest within ourselves and live more peaceably with others.

The psalmist used his experience to encourage all God's people to trust him.

It is good to hope in the Lord and quietly wait for his salvation throughout every trial.
classic_reading:
[Ps.131.1]
Chapter 131
The psalmist's humility. Believers encouraged to trust in God.
--The psalmist aimed at nothing high or great, but to be content in every condition God allotted. Humble saints cannot think so well of themselves as others think of them. The love of God reigning in the heart, will subdue self-love. Where there is a proud heart, there is commonly a proud look. To know God and our duty, is learning sufficiently high for us. It is our wisdom not to meddle with that which does not belong to us. He was well reconciled to every condition the Lord placed him in. He had been as humble as a little child about the age of weaning, and as far from aiming at high things; as entirely at God's disposal, as the child at the disposal of the mother or nurse. We must become as little children, [Matt.18.3] Mt 18:3. Our hearts are desirous of worldly things, cry for them, and are fond of them; but, by the grace of God, a soul that is made holy, is weaned from these things. The child is cross and fretful while in the weaning; but in a day or two it cares no longer for milk, and it can bear stronger food. Thus does a converted soul quiet itself under the loss of what it loved, and disappointments in what it hoped for, and is easy whatever happens. When our condition is not to our mind, we must bring our mind to our condition; then we are easy to ourselves and all about us; then our souls are as a weaned child. And thus the psalmist recommends confidence in God, to all the Israel of God, from his own experience. It is good to hope, and quietly to wait for the salvation of the Lord under every trial.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid's care for the ark.1–10The promises of God.11–18
David desires a dwelling place for the Lord (verses 1–10)

David committed himself to finding a place for the ark, the sign of God's presence.

When we have work to do for the Lord, it helps to set aside a time to do it.

Each morning we can plan the work of the day while submitting our plans to Providence, since we do not know what the day will bring.

Before anything else, let us seek without delay to have our hearts made God's dwelling place through the Holy Spirit.

David prayed that the Lord would inhabit the sanctuary prepared for him.

He also prayed that God would give the priests and other ministers grace to fulfill their duties.

David pleaded that he was the Lord's anointed, pointing forward to Christ, the great Anointed One.

We possess no merit of our own that would recommend us to God.

But Christ possesses an abundance of merit, and for his sake we ask to receive favor.

Every genuine believer is also anointed in Christ, receiving the grace of the Holy One.

Our prayer is that God will hear and answer for his Son's sake.

God's promise and the reign of Messiah (verses 11–18)

The Lord does not turn away those who plead his covenant through the Anointed Prophet, Priest and King.

What astonishing love God shows toward his church!

He desires to dwell with his people, while we desire so little to dwell with him.

He remained in Zion until Israel's sins led him to hand the city over to enemies.

Lord, although we too are sinful, do not abandon us.

God's people enjoy a special blessing even on life's ordinary comforts.

That blessing gives them an added sweetness.

Zion's poor may be content with little earthly wealth because far better treasures are prepared for them.

The Lord richly nourishes the new spiritual life, satisfying those poor in spirit with the bread of life.

He gives more than we ask.

When he gives salvation, he also grants abundant joy.

God would frustrate every attempt to destroy David's royal house until the King Messiah arose from it to sit upon his Father's throne.

All the promises are fulfilled in Christ.

Those who refuse to acknowledge his reign will finally face everlasting shame and confusion.

He prays that God would take up his dwelling in the habitation he had built; that he would give grace to the ministers of the sanctuary to do their duty. David pleads that he was the anointed of the Lord, and this he pleads as a type of Christ, the great Anointed. We have no merit of our own to plead; but, for His sake, in whom there is a fulness of merit, let us find favour. And every true believer in Christ, is an anointed one, and has received from the Holy One the oil of true grace. The request is, that God would not turn away, but hear and answer their petitions for his Son's sake.
[Ps.132.11-Ps.132.18]
Verses 11-18
The Lord never turns from us when we plead the covenant with his anointed Prophet, Priest, and King. How vast is the love of God to man, that he should speak thus concerning his church! It is his desire to dwell with us; yet how little do we desire to dwell with him! He abode in Zion till the sins of Israel caused him to give them up to the spoilers. Forsake us not, O God, and deliver us not in like manner, sinful though we are. God's people have a special blessing on common enjoyments, and that blessing puts peculiar sweetness into them. Zion's poor have reason to be content with a little of this world, because they have better things prepared for them. God will abundantly bless the nourishment of the new man, and satisfy the poor in spirit with the bread of life. He gives more than we ask, and when he gives salvation, he will give abundant joy. God would bring to nothing every design formed to destroy the house of David, until King Messiah should arise out of it, to sit upon the throne of his Father. In him all the promises centre. His enemies, who will not have him to reign over them, shall at the last day be clothed with shame and confusion for ever.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The excellency of brotherly love.

The blessing of living together in peace

We cannot say too much to encourage people to live in peace with one another.

Such peace is good for our dignity and comfort, and it gives continued joy to those who enjoy genuine unity.

The beauty of this fellowship is compared with the sacred anointing oil.

Brotherly love is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, evidence of union with Christ, and an adornment to the gospel.

It is not only pleasant but beneficial.

Its blessings are as numerous as drops of dew.

As dew cools the air and refreshes dry ground, love cools the burning heat of human anger.

It softens the heart and prepares it to receive and bear fruit from the seed of God's word.

The excellence of this love is confirmed by God's promise: where brothers and sisters live together in unity, the Lord commands his blessing.

Human beings can only request a blessing.

God commands it.

Believers who live in love and peace have the God of love and peace with them now.

Soon they will be with him forever in a world of perfect and unending peace.

May everyone who loves the Lord bear with and forgive one another, as God has forgiven them for Christ's sake.
classic_reading:
[Ps.133.1]
Chapter 133
The excellency of brotherly love.
--We cannot say too much, it were well if enough could be said, to persuade people to live together in peace. It is good for us, for our honour and comfort; and brings constant delight to those who live in unity. The pleasantness of this is likened to the holy anointing oil. This is the fruit of the Spirit, the proof of our union with Christ, and adorns his gospel. It is profitable as well as pleasing; it brings blessings numerous as the drops of dew. It cools the scorching heat of men's passions, as the dews cool the air and refresh the earth. It moistens the heart, and makes it fit to receive the good seed of the word, and to make it fruitful. See the proof of the excellency of brotherly love: where brethren dwell together in unity, the Lord commands the blessing. God commands the blessing; man can but beg a blessing. Believers that live in love and peace, shall have the God of love and peace with them now, and they shall shortly be with him for ever, in the world of endless love and peace. May all who love the Lord forbear and forgive one another, as God, for Christ's sake, hath forgiven them.

modern_osis:
Original heading

An exhortation to bless the Lord.

Using every available moment for praise

We should encourage our souls to give glory to God and to hope for his mercy and grace.

It is an excellent practice to fill otherwise unused moments with prayer, praise and godly meditation.

Then spare time need not become a burden.

We will not waste our hours on empty conversation, idle entertainment or indulgence of sinful desires.

The Lord's blessing is enough to make us happy.

We should pray for spiritual blessings not only for ourselves, but also for others.

Let our prayer be more than Lord, bless me.

Let us also say to another person, May the Lord bless you.

In doing so we declare that God has enough mercy for others as well as for us.

We also demonstrate genuine love and goodwill toward them.
classic_reading:
[Ps.134.1]
Chapter 134
An exhortation to bless the Lord.
--We must stir up ourselves to give glory to God, and encourage ourselves to hope for mercy and grace from him. It is an excellent plan to fill up all our spare minutes with pious meditations, and prayers and praises. No time would then be a burden, nor should we murder our hours by trifling conversation and vain amusements, or by carnal indulgences. We need desire no more to make us happy, than to be blessed of the Lord. We ought to beg spiritual blessings, not only for ourselves, but for others; not only, The Lord bless me, but, The Lord bless thee; thus testifying our belief that there is enough for others as well as for us, and showing our good will to others.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod to be praised for his mercy.1–4For his power and judgments.5–14The vanity of idols.15–21
Praising the Lord's gracious election (verses 1–4)

Our praise should center on the blessings of grace flowing from God's everlasting love.

We should love and honor his name because he is our covenant God and Father through Christ, blessing us with every spiritual blessing in him.

The Lord chose a people to belong to him, so that his name would be honored and praised through them.

If they fail to thank him for this special favor, they show extraordinary ingratitude and unworthiness.

God's power and faithfulness to his people (verses 5–14)

The Lord is, and will always be, the same gracious, faithful God who works wonders for his church.

And his church, in response, will remain a thankful people who praise him.

In this way his name endures through every generation.

He will return to his people with mercy and will delight in doing them good.

Rejecting idols and witnessing through a holy life (verses 15–21)

The psalm teaches believers to resist idolatry and false worship by showing what sort of gods the nations had been worshiping.

The more tragic their condition, the more thankful we should be that we have received a greater knowledge of God.

We ought to pity them, pray for them and seek their good, not treat them with contempt.

May we glorify God's name and commend his truth not merely through speech, but also through holy lives that imitate the goodness and faithfulness of Jesus Christ.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod to be praised as the Creator of the world.1–9As Israel's God and Saviour.10–22For his blessings to all.23–26
God's everlasting mercy in creation (verses 1–9)

We are so forgetful that we need to hear essential truths repeatedly. Here every refrain reminds us that God's mercy endures forever.

Mercy means more than a general disposition to kindness. It is the Lord's willingness to rescue people made miserable and vile through sin and includes everything he has provided to redeem sinners through Jesus Christ.

The purposes of that mercy are eternal. Its saving effects endure forever for those who receive it.

God remains as ready to show mercy to those who seek him as he ever was. This is the foundation of our comfort and hope.

God's saving mercy to Israel (verses 10–22)

The Lord's extraordinary works in bringing Israel out of Egypt were mercies whose benefits continued for generations.

The greater redemption accomplished by Christ, which those events pictured, endures forever.

We should examine the history of God's favors carefully, remembering in each event that his mercy lasts forever.

He brought Israel into a fruitful land. This too served as a picture of the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Mercy in every gift and all our praise (verses 23–26)

God's everlasting mercy is praised here in the deliverance of his church, in all his glorious works and in all the gifts he provides.

Blessed be God, who has made known and provided salvation through his Son.

May we know and experience his redeeming power, so that we serve him in righteousness throughout our lives.

The Lord gives food to every living creature. Let us ask him to feed our souls with eternal life and stir up our affections through grace, so that we thank and praise his holy name.

Trace every blessing to its true source, and keep offering him praise, for his mercy endures forever.

Forgetful as we are, things must be often repeated to us. By "mercy" we understand the Lord's disposition to save those whom sin has rendered miserable and vile, and all the provision he has made for the redemption of sinners by Jesus Christ. The counsels of this mercy have been from everlasting, and the effects of it will endure for ever, to all who are interested in it. The Lord continues equally ready to show mercy to all who seek for it, and this is the source of all our hope and comfort.
[Ps.136.10-Ps.136.22]
Verses 10-22
The great things God did for Israel, when he brought them out of Egypt, were mercies which endured long to them; and our redemption by Christ, which was typified thereby, endures for ever. It is good to enter into the history of God's favours, and in each to observe, and own, that his mercy endureth for ever. He put them in possession of a good land; it was a figure of the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.
[Ps.136.23-Ps.136.26]
Verses 23-26
God's everlasting mercy is here praised for the redemption of his church; in all his glories, and all his gifts. Blessed be God, who has provided and made known to us salvation through his Son. May we know and feel his redeeming power, that we may serve him in righteousness all our days. May He who giveth food to all flesh, feed our souls unto eternal life, and enliven our affections by his grace, that we may give thanks and praise to his holy name, for his mercy endureth for ever. Let us trace up all the favours we receive to this true source, and offer praise continually.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Jews bewail their captivity.1–4Their affection for Jerusalem.5–9
Refusing to turn Zion's songs into a mockery (verses 1–4)

The Jews' enemies had carried them captive into a foreign land.

They then added insult to their grief by demanding laughter and songs.

That cruelty was also profanity, because their captors wanted to hear the songs of Zion.

We should not comply with the demands of those who mock what is holy.

The captives were not merely saying they were too sad to sing. Their objection was that these were the Lord's songs, which they dared not offer as entertainment among idolaters.

Remembering Jerusalem and entrusting vengeance to God (verses 5–9)

We naturally think about what we truly love.

Those who rejoice in God make Jerusalem their joy for his sake.

The Jewish exiles resolved never to lose that affection.

During suffering, we should recall with godly sorrow the mercies we forfeited and the sins through which they were lost.

Far from taking private revenge, we must leave vengeance to the Lord, who has declared that it belongs to him.

People who rejoice in others' suffering, especially the calamities of Jerusalem, will not escape judgment.

We cannot pray for the promised success of God's church without looking toward the ruin of her enemies, even if we do not voice a prayer for that ruin.

Above all, remember that our hope of reaching the heavenly Jerusalem rests entirely on God's grace and Christ's finished salvation.

Verses 1-4
Their enemies had carried the Jews captive from their own land. To complete their woes, they insulted over them; they required of them mirth and a song. This was very barbarous; also profane, for no songs would serve but the songs of Zion. Scoffers are not to be compiled with. They do not say, How shall we sing, when we are so much in sorrow? but, It is the Lord's song, therefore we dare not sing it among idolaters.
[Ps.137.5-Ps.137.9]
Verses 5-9
What we love, we love to think of. Those that rejoice in God, for his sake make Jerusalem their joy. They stedfastly resolved to keep up this affection. When suffering, we should recollect with godly sorrow our forfeited mercies, and our sins by which we lost them. If temporal advantages ever render a profession, the worst calamity has befallen him. Far be it from us to avenge ourselves; we will leave it to Him who has said, Vengeance is mine. Those that are glad at calamities, especially at the calamities of Jerusalem, shall not go unpunished. We cannot pray for promised success to the church of God without looking to, though we do not utter a prayer for, the ruin of her enemies. But let us call to mind to whose grace and finished salvation alone it is, that we have any hopes of being brought home to the heavenly Jerusalem.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist praises God for answering prayer.1–5The Lord's dealing with the humble and the proud.6–8
Wholehearted thanks for answered prayer (verses 1–5)

When we can praise the Lord with all our hearts, we should not hesitate to let the whole world see our gratitude and joy.

Those who depend on God's lovingkindness and truth through Jesus Christ will always find him faithful to his word.

If God did not spare his own Son, will he not also freely give us all things with him?

The Lord may strengthen our souls even while outward affliction remains.

He gives us grace to carry burdens, withstand temptation and fulfill our duties.

He strengthens us to hold firmly to him by faith and wait patiently for the outcome.

Such grace deserves our sincere thanksgiving.

His mercy to the humble and distance from the proud (verses 6–8)

Although the Lord is exalted, he regards every humble sinner.

The proud and unbelieving, however, will be excluded from his blessed presence.

God's consolations can revive us even in the middle of suffering.

He saves his people so that the Holy Spirit, the giver of life and holiness, can renew them.

When we give God glory for his mercy, we may receive the comfort of that mercy ourselves.

Confidence in his promises should increase our prayers, not make us stop praying.

Any good present in us is the Lord's work.

He works within his people both to will and to act.

He will complete the salvation of every genuine believer and will not abandon those whom he has made new in Christ Jesus for good works.
classic_reading:

Chapter 138

When we can praise God with our whole heart, we need not be unwilling for the whole world to witness our gratitude and joy in him. If God gives us strength in our souls, to bear the burdens, resist the temptations, and to do the duties of an afflicted state, if he strengthens us to keep hold of himself by faith, and to wait with patience for the event, we are bound to be thankful.

The Lord will perfect the salvation of every true believer, and he will never forsake those whom he has created anew in Christ Jesus unto good works.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod knows all things.1–6He is every where present.7–16The psalmist's hatred to sin, and desire to be led aright.17–24
The Lord knows every thought (verses 1–6)

God possesses perfect knowledge of all we think and do.

It is better to meditate upon this truth and apply it to our own lives in prayer than merely to dispute about it out of curiosity.

Everyone readily acknowledges God's omniscience—his knowledge of all things—and omnipresence—his presence everywhere.

Yet few live as though they really believe them.

The Lord notices every step, whether right or wrong.

He knows what rule guides us, where we are heading and whose company we seek.

When we withdraw from everyone else, he knows our inward life.

Before we speak a good or empty word, he knows the thoughts and intentions from which it arises.

Wherever we are, we live beneath his eye and within reach of his hand.

We cannot explain fully how he knows us so thoroughly.

This truth should restrain us from sin.

No darkness hides us or separates us from his care (verses 7–16)

We cannot see God, but he sees us.

The psalmist did not really want to escape the Lord.

He asked where anyone could go to leave God's presence.

Neither the furthest parts of the world nor heaven nor hell lie beyond his reach.

No veil of darkness hides an action or person from him.

Even secret wrongdoing is as plain before him as evil committed in daylight.

But this is also a great encouragement.

No suffering or location can remove the believer from the supporting and comforting presence of the almighty Friend.

If a persecutor kills a believer's body, the soul will all the sooner enter heaven.

Even the grave cannot separate the body from the Savior's love.

He will raise the body in glory.

No outward circumstance can ultimately divide the believer from the Lord.

Those who continue doing their duty may find joy in faith, hope and prayer wherever they are.

God's precious thoughts and a prayer for a cleansed heart (verses 17–24)

God's plans for his people are too deep for us to search out.

We cannot count his many mercies.

What a help it would be in keeping us reverent toward the Lord throughout the day if our first thoughts each morning were of him!

And how much more will we praise him when we awaken in the world of glory!

Our bodies were wonderfully formed.

We should never use their members or senses as instruments of sin.

Our immortal, rational souls are even greater gifts.

Yet if God had not loved sinners, our reason and immortality would make our guilt and eternal loss all the more dreadful.

Let us therefore meditate with delight upon God's love to sinners in Jesus Christ, which surpasses calculation.

People who fear God hate sin, but grieve for sinners.

Even when they avoid their wrongdoing, they should pray for their conversion and salvation, because God can accomplish both.

The Lord knows us fully, while we know ourselves only imperfectly.

Ask him through his word and Spirit to search and test our hearts.

If any wicked way is within us, may he show it and remove it.

The old and good way of godliness is pleasing to God, beneficial to us and leads to everlasting life.

All saints want to remain on that path without wandering away or growing weary.
classic_reading:
[Ps.139.1-Ps.139.6]
Chapter 139
Chapter Outline
God knows all things. | (1-6) |
He is every where present. | (7-16) |
The psalmist's hatred to sin, and desire to be led aright. | (17-24) |
Verses 1-6
God has perfect knowledge of us, and all our thoughts and actions are open before him. It is more profitable to meditate on Divine truths, applying them to our own cases, and with hearts lifted to God in prayer, than with a curious or disputing frame of mind. That God knows all things, is omniscient; that he is every where, is omnipresent; are truths acknowledged by all, yet they are seldom rightly believed in by mankind. God takes strict notice of every step we take, every right step and every by step. He knows what rule we walk by, what end we walk toward, what company we walk with. When I am withdrawn from all company, thou knowest what I have in my heart. There is not a vain word, not a good word, but thou knowest from what thought it came, and with what design it was uttered. Wherever we are, we are under the eye and hand of God. We cannot by searching find how God searches us out; nor do we know how we are known. Such thoughts should restrain us from sin.
[Ps.139.7-Ps.139.16]
Verses 7-16
We cannot see God, but he can see us. The psalmist did not desire to go from the Lord. Whither can I go? In the most distant corners of the world, in heaven, or in hell, I cannot go out of thy reach. No veil can hide us from God; not the thickest darkness. No disguise can save any person or action from being seen in the true light by him. Secret haunts of sin are as open before God as the most open villanies. On the other hand, the believer cannot be removed from the supporting, comforting presence of his Almighty Friend. Should the persecutor take his life, his soul will the sooner ascend to heaven. The grave cannot separate his body from the love of his Saviour, who will raise it a glorious body. No outward circumstances can separate him from his Lord. While in the path of duty, he may be happy in any situation, by the exercise of faith, hope, and prayer.
[Ps.139.17-Ps.139.24]
Verses 17-24
God's counsels concerning us and our welfare are deep, such as cannot be known. We cannot think how many mercies we have received from him. It would help to keep us in the fear of the Lord all the day long, if, when we wake in the morning, our first thoughts were of him: and how shall we admire and bless our God for his precious salvation, when we awake in the world of glory! Surely we ought not to use our members and senses, which are so curiously fashioned, as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin. But our immortal and rational souls are a still more noble work and gift of God. Yet if it were not for his precious thoughts of love to us, our reason and our living for ever would, through our sins, prove the occasion of our eternal misery. How should we then delight to meditate on God's love to sinners in Jesus Christ, the sum of which exceeds all reckoning! Sin is hated, and sinners lamented, by all who fear the Lord. Yet while we shun them we should pray for them; with God their conversion and salvation are possible. As the Lord knows us thoroughly, and we are strangers to ourselves, we should earnestly desire and pray to be searched and proved by his word and Spirit. if there be any wicked way in me, let me see it; and do thou root it out of me. The way of godliness is pleasing to God, and profitable to us; and will end in everlasting life. It is the good old way. All the saints desire to be kept and led in this way, that they may not miss it, turn out of it, or tire in it.

Praying for protection from open and hidden danger (verses 1–7)

The greater the danger, the more seriously we should turn to God in prayer.

Everyone sheltered by the Lord is safe.

If God is for us, who can be against us?

We should especially watch and pray that the Lord will establish our steps in his ways and keep us from stumbling.

God is just as able to preserve his servants from hidden deceit as from open violence.

Our experience of his care in one danger should strengthen our confidence that he will help in other dangers too.

The Lord's judgment and the righteousness of Christ (verses 8–13)

Believers may rightly pray that God will not grant the desires of wicked people or help their evil schemes succeed.

Those who make false accusations bring their own trouble upon themselves, even the fiery coals of divine judgment.

The righteous will dwell before God and thank him forever.

Real thanksgiving must become thanks-living.

Every deliverance should move us to serve the Lord more faithfully and cheerfully.

Those who are slandered or mistreated by others can nevertheless be accepted as righteous before God.

That is possible only through the righteousness of Jesus Christ, imputed to them and received through faith.

Its effect in their lives is that they begin to live self-controlled, upright lives.

They give thanks to God for the righteousness by which they are counted righteous and for every gift of grace and mercy they receive.

[Ps.140.1-Ps.140.7]
Chapter 140
Chapter Outline
David encourages himself in God. | (1-7) |
He prays for, and prophesies the destruction of, his persecutors. | (8-13) |
Verses 1-7
The more danger appears, the more earnest we should be in prayer to God. All are safe whom the Lord protects. If he be for us, who can be against us? We should especially watch and pray, that the Lord would hold up our goings in his ways, that our footsteps slip not. God is as able to keep his people from secret fraud as from open force; and the experience we have had of his power and care, in dangers of one kind, may encourage us to depend upon him in other dangers.
[Ps.140.8-Ps.140.13]
Verses 8-13
Believers may pray that God would not grant the desires of the wicked, nor further their evil devices. False accusers will bring mischief upon themselves, even the burning coals of Divine vengeance. And surely the righteous shall dwell in God's presence, and give him thanks for evermore. This is true thanksgiving, even thanks-living: this use we should make of all our deliverances, we should serve God the more closely and cheerfully. Those who, though evil spoken of and ill-used by men, are righteous in the sight of God, being justified by the righteousness of Christ, which is imputed to them, and received by faith, as the effect of which, they live soberly and righteously; these give thanks to the Lord, for the righteousness whereby they are made righteous, and for every blessing of grace, and mercy of life.
